frameworks.name: Business Model Difficulty Curves
frameworks.definition: Each major business model (Info, SaaS, E-commerce, Service) has a characteristic shape: startup speed, scalability trajectory, and the dominant constraint (people, cash flow, retention, talent) that emerges at each stage.

frameworks.name: Demand vs. Supply Constraint Framework
frameworks.definition: Businesses face either demand constraints (can acquire more customers than can be served) or supply constraints (cannot hire talent fast enough to serve existing demand); this industry-level pattern predicts difficulty and hiring challenge severity.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that $10 million annual revenue is achievable in nearly any business model, with the exception of brick-and-mortar with constrained local markets (fewer than ~100 local customers), by opening additional geographic locations and maintaining the same repeatable unit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Non-brick-and-mortar businesses
Willingness to expand to new markets
40+ year time horizon
bounded_by: Does not apply to brick-and-mortar businesses in very small markets (fewer than 100 local customers available)

claims.text: Most founders abandon their current business prematurely, not because the business model is wrong, but because they are impatient and believe a different opportunity will succeed faster; Hormozi argues that maintaining focus through one business for 40 years would likely succeed, making commitment a stronger lever than opportunity-switching.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The core business model is fundamentally sound (no structural assumption error)
Skill development is not the binding constraint
claims.mechanism: Opportunity-switching incurs a compounding time penalty: a new business starts at year one while the abandoned business continues growing; even if the new business has a higher growth rate initially, the head start compounds, keeping the founder behind indefinitely

anchors.value: year 1, even if growth rate is higher
current business at year 5, new business still at year 2

bounded_by: Does not apply when there is a fundamental assumption error in the business model
Does not apply when the required skill is the binding growth constraint (though Hormozi argues this is rare)

claims.text: Founders frequently mistake business-model features (inherent structural difficulties) for bugs (fixable defects), then abandon their business; in reality, every business model has a characteristic difficulty that is the source of competitive moat and profit, not a sign of failure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The business is on its natural maturation curve
No fundamental assumption error has been discovered
claims.mechanism: The presence of a difficulty signals why the business generates profit: only businesses with difficulty are compensated. If something is easy, many competitors enter and erode margins. Difficulty preserves pricing power.

claims.text: Cleaning businesses face a primary constraint of attracting and retaining high-quality service delivery talent; fitness coaching businesses face the opposite constraint of customer retention, as customers struggle with goal adherence and cancel frequently.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service-based business model
Observable customer cohort behavior
claims.mechanism: In cleaning, the service is easy (customers want it, renew automatically), so the difficulty is finding people to do the work. In fitness, the service is hard to stay committed to (customers lack motivation), so the difficulty is retaining customers, not talent.
bounded_by: Fitness coaching example specific to weight-loss coaching; other fitness verticals may differ

claims.text: Accounting firms exhibit the opposite constraint pattern from cleaning businesses: high customer annual retention ("super high annual stick") combined with severe talent acquisition difficulty, because accounting skill is scarce and in-demand across multiple industries.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Professional service business (accounting)
claims.mechanism: High skill barrier to entry creates supply constraint: few people can do the work, so talent is scarce. Customers, on the other hand, have few options and remain sticky because of switching costs and regulatory/compliance requirements.

claims.text: In weight-loss coaching services, it is easy to attract high-quality talent because many people are intrinsically motivated by fitness and nutrition topics; however, customer retention is extremely difficult because people struggle with diet adherence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Weight-loss or fitness coaching service industry
Intrinsic motivation present in the talent pool
claims.mechanism: People are willing to work in fitness for below-market compensation because they are passionate about the domain, creating a talent supply that exceeds demand. However, customers cancel because goal-adherence is difficult.
bounded_by: Specific to weight-loss and fitness verticals where intrinsic motivation is high

claims.text: When many people want to work in an industry, there is intense competition among service providers, low barriers to entry, and therefore customers have abundant options and low switching costs; the inverse holds when talent is scarce.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service industry with open competition
claims.mechanism: Supply of labor inversely correlates with customer retention and pricing power: abundant labor creates a buyer's market for customers (low switching costs, abundant alternatives), while scarce labor creates a seller's market and high customer stickiness.

claims.text: A founder operating counter to their industry's baseline constraint (e.g., supply-constrained cleaning business with abundant talent, or demand-constrained software with labor challenges) is either executing something exceptionally right or exceptionally wrong; this deviation signals unusual performance, not normal operation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The business does not match the industry's structural constraint pattern
claims.mechanism: Industry constraints are structural; matching them indicates normal execution. Mismatching signals either superior execution or fundamental misalignment.

claims.text: Founders without experience frequently interpret their business's structural difficulty as a sign of failure and pivot prematurely; they then spend multiple years half-committed to multiple opportunities while blaming growth shortfalls on business model failure, rather than on their divided attention.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder is inexperienced / lacks pattern recognition
Structural difficulty has emerged as expected
claims.mechanism: Split focus compounds disadvantageously: growth when smaller is harder than growth when larger, so divided attention in year 1-3 prevents reaching the inflection point where growth accelerates. The founder then attributes slow growth to business model failure rather than execution failure.

claims.text: Info product businesses (coaching, education, SaaS courses) have a characteristic shape of fast initial growth ("make a million dollars really quickly") followed by severe scaling difficulty because revenue retention is near zero; once customers learn the content, they graduate and leave.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Info product or coaching business model
Knowledge-transfer-based value prop
claims.mechanism: Customers consume the product (learning), complete the journey (graduation), and have no reason to retain. Retention-free model requires constant new customer acquisition to maintain growth.

claims.text: SaaS (software) businesses exhibit the opposite curve from info products: slow, unprofitable startup (low ticket price, extended development timelines, talent acquisition difficulty), followed by explosive scalability once product-market fit is achieved, often taking years to reach profitability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) business model
claims.mechanism: Software requires high upfront R&D investment with deferred monetization (long sales cycle, low initial price, high customer acquisition cost), but achieving scale unlocks efficient unit economics through recurring revenue and zero-marginal-cost distribution.

anchors.value: can scale to very large revenues

claims.text: E-commerce businesses face a characteristic constraint of cash flow management: rapid scaling requires continuous inventory replenishment, supplier relationship management, and logistics scaling (3PL changes, volume threshold adjustments), creating a compounding operational burden at each growth inflection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: E-commerce / product sales business model
Growth phase requiring inventory scaling
claims.mechanism: Growth revenue is not liquid growth: each dollar in new revenue requires capital to fund inventory, and growing order volumes require switching logistics partners and managing more supplier relationships, creating operational complexity.

claims.text: Service businesses grow the slowest of all major models (info, SaaS, e-commerce, service), but the growth is the steadiest and most predictable; the constraint is people (hiring, training, retention), not cash flow or product development.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service-based business model
People-intensive delivery
claims.mechanism: Service growth is bounded by hiring and training velocity because each new customer requires additional headcount; this creates predictability (growth = hiring × productivity) and eliminates cash-flow and product-iteration friction.

claims.text: The founder bias toward diversification and adding secondary service lines often dilutes focus and slows the primary business; sticking with a single, refined service model compounds faster than splitting effort across multiple offerings.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multiple service lines or offerings in the same business
Primary line is fundable to $10M+ independently
claims.mechanism: Effort is zero-sum: time spent scaling a secondary line is time not spent deepening the primary line's moat, customer base, or delivery excellence.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the primary line has a ceiling and the secondary line is genuinely necessary for diversification

claims.text: Founders who maintain long-term commitment to a single business (a 40-year horizon) achieve faster growth than those who hold one business for 2-3 years and then jump; the compounding benefit of the head start outweighs higher growth rates from switching.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: No structural assumption error in the business
40+ year time horizon is viable for the founder
claims.mechanism: Growth compounds: a 3-year head start on a business with even modest growth rate (10-20% annually) creates a gap that is never closed by a new business with higher growth rate (25-30%), because time-weighted cumulative growth favors early starts.

examples.text: A founder in year 3 of a current business considers switching to a new opportunity that appears to have higher growth potential in year 1. Even if the new business grows 30-50% faster than the old business, by the time the founder is in year 5 of the new opportunity, they are actually still behind: the old business would be at year 8 of its cumulative growth, while the new business is still at year 2. Growth compounds, so the head start is never recoverable.

A founder with a wandering eye abandons a marriage (or business) repeatedly to pursue what appears to be a better opportunity, yet spends all their energy looking rather than doubling down. The result is a weak marriage and no alternative relationship; the same applies to business: divided attention prevents reaching the inflection point where the original business compounds.

practices.text: When evaluating a business difficulty or apparent flaw, ask: is this a feature (structural characteristic of this business model that creates the moat) or a bug (a fixable defect)? Most founders mistake features for bugs and abandon their business prematurely.

Before switching to a new business, verify that you have discovered a fundamental assumption error or that skill is genuinely the binding constraint. If neither is true, stay committed to the current business for at least 3-5 more years.

Analyze your industry's baseline constraint (demand vs. supply) and check whether your business matches. If you are mismatched, it is a signal to investigate whether you are executing exceptionally (above-market advantage) or exceptionally poorly (fundamental misalignment).
